Deep DIC Code Audit

Deep DIC Code Audit

None of the four notebooks could run. They do now, and I trained both networks on synthetic data to see what the pipeline produces. DisplacementNet learned. StrainNet did not get past predicting zero in the time available.

Repository: Deep-Dic-deep-learning-based-digital-image-correlation, branch main, 2 November 2026. Measured on a 10-core Intel Core Ultra 5 225 with no GPU.

4 of 4notebooks now run start to finish. 24 blocking failures fixed; 30 of 30 behaviour checks pass.
0.48 pxDisplacementNet mean error on unseen images. Predicting zero scores 1.67 px.
1.97%StrainNet mean error, level with predicting zero at 1.99%.
3.5×higher error from the missing fcn.eval(), the worst bug that gives no warning.

These numbers test the pipeline. They do not measure Deep DIC's accuracy. The authors' dataset and weights are not in the repository, so I generated 3,600 image pairs from the paper's Tables 1 and 2. DisplacementNet then saw 6,888 training images on a CPU, about 1,045 times fewer than the 7.2 million in the paper's 200 epochs. The fixed notebooks have not yet been run on the authors' data.

What stopped the notebooks

Each failure hid the next one, so I fixed one at a time and reran until the notebook finished. The table for each notebook lists every failure in the order it appeared. The count of 24 includes placeholder names that needed real paths and GPU-only calls that fail on this CPU, so not every entry is a coding error.

Bugs that give wrong numbers without crashing

These are more dangerous than the crashes, because the code would have kept running. All are now fixed.

Inference without fcn.eval()

Mean displacement error on 150 unseen pairs, px

Light dims 20% between two frames

Mean displacement error on 150 unseen pairs, px

BugEffect
Run notebooks never called fcn.eval()Error rose from 0.47 to 1.61 px, almost as bad as no model. Each frame also overwrites the stored BatchNorm statistics, so the damage persists: 1.36 px even after switching to eval mode.
Validation images were also training imagesAll 4,000 validation images were in the training list, while the provided split files went unused. The two split files share no images. In this short run the leak made no measurable difference (28.5% of the zero-output error on unseen images, 29.1% on training images), because the network had not started to overfit. It would matter in a full run.
Fixed learning rateThe paper drops the rate 100×. Doing so cut validation MSE 64%, from 4.93 to 1.78, in 4 minutes of training.
Saved displacement not rescaledFor the example ROI of 366×190, resized to 384×192, saved values were 4.9% too large vertically and 1.1% too large horizontally.
StrainNet_run divided image 2 by image 1's maximumError doubled to 0.94 px when the light dimmed between frames. Dividing each image by its own maximum kept it at 0.47 px.
Rebuilt file lists never reached the data loadersThe lists rebuilt inside the training cells had no effect, because the loaders were already built from the old paths.
Logs and checkpoints in the wrong folderA missing path separator produced results/loglog_*.txt and results/modelparam_*.pth. Your results/ folder still holds ten of those log files.
Unreadable labels replaced by zerosThe fallback created a zero array of the wrong size. It now reports the real file error.
ROI corners rounded two waysnp.int truncated two corners and round rounded the other two, so the ROI size could change by a pixel per frame.

Reading the displacement result

DisplacementNet's mean error was 0.48 px (0.52 px horizontally, 0.43 px vertically), with a typical worst pixel of 3.6 px per image. Farneback optical flow, a classical method with no training, reached 0.06 px, 7.6 times better. So this short run is far from competitive. My synthetic images also suit optical flow: they are clean, and the deformation is smooth and small.

Why StrainNet did not learn

A flat loss can mean a bug, so I checked three things separately.

QuestionResultConclusion
Are the strain labels right?Strain differentiated from optical flow correlates with them at 0.86 or higher on all four channels.Labels and channel order are consistent
Did the trained network learn?Its predictions correlate with the labels at 0.16 at best, and they vary far less (standard deviation 0.19 against 2.53).Output is nearly constant
Can the pipeline learn at all?On 12 fixed images, loss fell from 6.08 to 0.025, or 99.6% lower, in 240 steps.The code path works

So the pipeline is sound and the 591 training steps were too few. Strain needs the difference in displacement between nearby points, which is a harder signal to learn than overall motion. This rules out a broken pipeline, but it does not prove that full training will reach the paper's accuracy. Only a longer run can show that.

Strain on the median sample

Strain
−101 %
Absolute error
02 %

Differentiating the network's displacement output gave 7.95% error, 4.0 times worse than predicting zero, because differentiation amplifies pixel-level noise. The paper makes the same point in favour of predicting strain directly, but this run cannot confirm the benefit, because StrainNet itself did not learn.

Where the code differs from the paper

Only the training schedule was changed. Changing the network or its outputs would break the published pretrained weights, so those are left as committed.

ItemPaperCodeAction
Training200 epochs, rate 1e-3 then 1e-5 after 100100 epochs, fixed rateChanged to match the paper
ActivationLeakyReLU, slope 0.01ReLULeft as is
Skip connectionsConcatenationAdditionLeft as is
StrainNet outputThree strains at full sizeFour displacement gradients at half sizeLeft as is
Rotation in strain labelsRemovedKept, as raw gradients include itLeft as is
LossMSE ×10 for displacement, ×100 for strainPlain MSE, with strain labels ×100Left as is
Output fieldsAccumulated over the sequenceSaved per frame pairLeft as is

The network has 50.0 million parameters and needs 11.9 billion multiply-accumulate operations per 128×128 pair. Inputs must be multiples of 32 pixels in both directions. 522,408 parameters in conv1 and fc are never used, but they must stay for the pretrained weights to load.

Still to check with the authors' data

  1. ROI direction. Diaplacement_run moves the ROI by minus the predicted displacement. The paper's description suggests plus. With a wrong sign, a sample moving 3 px per frame would leave the ROI 60 px off after 10 frames. I could not read Eq. 1 from the PDF and left the code unchanged. To test it, shift an image by a known amount and check the sign of the output.
  2. Strain channel order. np.gradient returns the row derivative first, so the channel named dudx is really ∂u/∂row if channel 0 is horizontal. A pure stretch u = 0.01x gives 0 in dudx and 0.01 in dudy. I kept the order for the pretrained weights and documented it in the notebooks, so read strain[1] and strain[2] as the normal strains until you have confirmed this.
  3. Image format. The loaders now convert images to 8-bit greyscale. That matches two-channel input, but I could not inspect the authors' files.
  4. README. It lists PyTorch 1.16, which does not exist. The paper says 1.6.0. I left the README unchanged. requirements.txt now lists the versions tested here.

Run it again

Everything here regenerates from analysis_results/code. You need the packages in requirements.txt.

python gen_data.py 3600        # synthetic dataset, about 1 minute and 2.2 GB
python train.py disp 25 4      # 25 minutes at the notebook rate, 4 at the low rate
python train.py strain 25 4
python evaluate.py             # test-set metrics and bug measurements
python strain_diagnose.py      # the StrainNet checks
